title: Fractured stream protocol and SDK adaptor playbook
content:
Overview

This doc is a working PRD / playbook hybrid exploring a "fractured stream" approach to hosted API streaming that prioritizes robust SDK ergonomics for tool-calling and typed structured output. The intent is to produce a developer-friendly surface that tolerates intermittent networks, supports partial tool results, and exposes clear telemetery hooks for rollouts. Not a finished spec — more of a concrete set of proposals, examples, and tradeoffs we can iterate on in the coming sprint.

Why 'fractured stream'?
- Many client applications need progressive signal (partial text + interim tool outputs) but cannot accept a single monolithic stream that blocks for large tool responses or retries.
- 'Fractured' emphasizes explicit boundaries: we deliver ordered fragments (frames) with typed envelopes and per-frame life-cycle metadata so SDKs can reconcile, hedge, or display partial outputs gracefully.

Problem statement
- Current streaming models conflate generator text and tool outputs in freeform token streams, making it hard for mobile/embedded SDKs to implement deterministic reconcilation and for devs to reason about partial results, retries, and costs.
- Tool calls (e.g., DB fetch, search, code-run) often produce results slower than text generation but are semantically richer — we need a way to present them without stalling user-visible text.
- Offline or flaky networks require resumable semantics and cheap fallbacks.

Goals (what success looks like)
- SDKs can reconstruct a deterministic transcript and tool-event timeline even with dropped connections.
- Frontend clients can show incremental text while tooling results arrive as separately addressable frames.
- Low-friction migration for current hosted-API users (no dramatic change to simple sync endpoints).
- Observability for both token-level cost and frame-level latencies and error classes.

Constraints
- Backwards compatibility: we must support existing non-fractured streaming for simple use-cases.
- Latency SLOs: streaming should not add >10ms median overhead for small responses.
- Payload size: frame metadata must be tiny and compressible.
- Security: tool frames may contain sensitive artifacts; we must preserve tokenization and KMS boundaries for private deployments.

High level approach
- Represent the response as an ordered sequence of frames (frame = small JSON envelope + optional payload chunk).
- Frames have three orthogonal axes: stream_kind (text | tool_event | schema_anchor), life_phase (draft | committed | retract), and wire_id (monotonic per-session id).
- Clients can subscribe to kinds of frames and display/act accordingly.
- A thin negotiation header (at session start) communicates which frame kinds and telemetry hooks a client wants.

Frame model (simple)
- Frame fields (kept minimal): frame_id, prev_frame_id, kind, phase, timestamp, signature (small stream-logic token), payload_type, payload (string/JSON/bytes-base64). All fields are strings except we keep timestamps as ISO-8601 strings.
- Examples of kinds: text-delta, tool-call-start, tool-call-progress, tool-call-result, structured-block, error-note, checkpoint.

Lifecycle semantics
- Draft: optimistic content that can be shown but not persisted as final.
- Committed: canonical content; SDK should mark earlier draft frames replaced/endorsed.
- Retract: indicates previously emitted content must be removed (rare but required for safety rollbacks).

Tool-calling specifics
- Tool calls are first-class frames with their own sub-streams. Pattern: tool-call-start -> zero or more tool-call-progress -> tool-call-result | tool-call-error.
- tool-call-start includes tool metadata (tool-id, version, input-hash) so that SDKs can dedupe or resume.
- tool-call-result payloads should prefer typed JSON for known tool contracts, fallback to base64 for opaque blobs.
- Tool frames must carry optional 'cost_estimate' and 'compute_profile' strings so downstream analytics can model unit economics.

Structured output and schema anchors
- For structured outputs we use schema_anchor frames with a stable schema_id. Anchors are emitted initially as 'schema_anchor:draft' and later committed.
- We recommend a lightweight versioning rule: schema_id = sha1(schema-json)+short-version. Avoid embedding full schemas in each frame; include a CDN-hosted schema link in negotiation headers.

SDK ergonomics (principles)
1) Local-first: SDKs present committed frames as primary, fall back to draft for progressive UX.
2) Idempotency: wire_id + session_id + frame_sequence enable exact replay semantics.
3) Small API surface: a single 'subscribe' event stream with typed callbacks; avoid multiple orthogonal streaming APIs.
4) Replay-friendly: SDK should be able to request frames starting at N given a server-supplied resume-token.
5) Minimal cognitive load: expose helper utilities like 'getLatestCommittedText()' and 'listActiveToolCalls()' rather than requiring app logic to parse frames.

SDK API sketch (pseudo JS)
- Connect: const s = new StreamClient({sessionToken, want: ['text-delta', 'tool-call-result', 'schema_anchor']})
- Events: s.on('frame', (frame) => { switch(frame.kind){ case 'text-delta': ui.appendDraft(frame.payload); break; case 'tool-call-start': ui.showToolSpinner(frame.frame_id); break; case 'tool-call-result': ui.replaceSpinnerWithToolOutput(frame.frame_id, frame.payload); break; }})
- Resume: s.resume({resumeToken}) -> server streams frames from resume point.

Buffering & backpressure
- SDKs should implement two logical buffers: display buffer (fast, bounded) and reconciliation buffer (full fidelity). Server will emit small text-delta frames (<1KB) frequently. Large tool payloads are chunked as multiple frames.
- Backpressure strategy: client sends a small credit window in the negotiation header; server respects it (useful for low-memory devices).

Partial / graceful degradation strategies
- If tool result is delayed beyond threshold, emit a 'tool-call-timeout' soft-frame suggesting the client show a cached or stubbed result. This is a visual hint only; the authoritative tool-call-result may arrive later.
- For intermittent networks, client can request trimmed resume (headers only) to quickly get frame metadata and then request full payloads lazily.

Observability & telemetry
- Per-frame tags: server emits latency_class and cost_bucket as tags.
- SDKs send metrics: frame_receive_time, frame_apply_time, reconcilation_errors, tool_call_late_arrivals.
- Use aggregated histograms (p95/p99) on tool result arrival latencies to tune default hedging thresholds.

Migration story (compatibility)
- Continue supporting the current streaming API in parallel. New fractured stream is opt-in via a session header: "X-Prefer-Fractured: 1".
- For simple text-only callers we return text-delta frames that canonicalize into one committed response so nothing breaks.

Edge-cases and failure modes
- Out-of-order arrival: frames include prev_frame_id; SDK should buffer up to a short window (configurable) and request missing frames from the server if gaps persist.
- Replay collisions: if a client simultaneously performs a replay while the server performs a canary rollback, we must include a global session_version token that invalidates older sequences.
- Large binary payloads from tools: use CDN-hosted URIs in frames with signed short-lived tokens instead of embedding heavy bytes.

Security and privacy considerations
- Tool payloads must be classified at emission (sensitive | non-sensitive). For private deployments we enforce KMS policies and never emit sensitive payloads in cleartext frames — instead emit placeholder and a secure artifact reference.
- Frame-level audit logs for compliance: committed frames should be retained in audit logs with consistent IDs referencing session and model version.

Open questions (for the next sync)
- Should we support multiple parallel tool substreams per session or limit to a single tool-chain to simplify ordering?
- What are reasonable default hedging thresholds per tool type (search vs code-run vs DB lookup)?
- How do we best compress successive text-deltas for low-bandwidth clients without increasing merge complexity?

API example (minimal HTTP/WS handshake)
- Client start: POST /v1/sessions { model: "x", fractured: true, want: ["text-delta","tool-call-*"], client_capabilities: {resume: true,credit_window: 8} }
- Server responds: 200 {session_id, resume_token, supported_kinds:[...], schema_catalog:[url1,url2]}
- WS frames: framed-JSON chunks, newline delimited. Example frame:
  {"frame_id":"0001","prev_frame_id":"","kind":"text-delta","phase":"draft","timestamp":"2026-03-11T16:23:12Z","payload_type":"text","payload":"Hi — here's the start..."}

Rollout plan (minimal)
- Phase 0: internal SDK + integration tests (2 sprints).
- Phase 1: opt-in public beta for PLG customers (select teams), collect p95 tool latencies and SDK errors (1 month).
- Phase 2: default for new sessions, keep compatibility translation for legacy clients (2 months).

Next steps / action items
- Product: narrow hedging defaults and finalize negotiation header fields (owner: Maya, due: 2026-03-20).
- Eng serving-runtime: prototype frame router and resume-token mechanism (owner: Diego, spike due: 2026-03-18).
- SDK: implement reference JS and Kotlin adapters with helper utils (owner: Hannah, initial PR due: 2026-03-30).

Notes to reviewers
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and small: aim for forward-compatible primitives rather than a heavy rigid spec. Expect several follow-ups: a compact wire spec, schema registry decisions, and an SDK API README.
- I'm particularly interested in feedback around: resume semantics, backpressure ergonomics for mobile, and the privacy model for tool payloads.
